analysis.one_liner: Expands unpaid family and medical leave rights to workers at businesses with 25 or more employees.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have extended family and medical leave protections to roughly 13 million more workers, was referred to committee on January 22, 1997 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 1993 Family and Medical Leave Act lets covered workers take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for a new baby, a serious illness, or a sick family member, and guarantees they get their job back. But it only applies to employers with 50 or more employees at or near a worksite, which leaves out nearly half the private workforce. This bill would lower that threshold to 25 employees, bringing about 13 million additional workers under the law's protections. It never got a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at companies with 25 to 49 employees who need time off for their own serious health condition, a new child, or a sick family member. Today those workers can be fired simply for taking the time; the bill would guarantee them 12 weeks of unpaid leave and the right to return to their job.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Family and Medical Leave Act to cover employers with 25 or more employees at a worksite and within 75 miles of it, down from 50 [S2] [S3].

The bill's own findings state that 13 million additional private employees, about 14 percent of the private workforce, would gain coverage, raising the protected share of the private workforce from 57 percent [S3].
The findings also note that between January 1994 and June 1995, 12 million employees took protected family and medical leave, showing the existing law was being used at scale [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 25 to 49 employees, who would have to track leave eligibility, hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, and absorb the absence of a worker on leave. The bill's findings cite employer surveys reporting that over 90 percent of covered employers experienced little or no cost and found compliance easy and inexpensive, and that smaller employers actually complied more cheaply than larger ones [S3].

drawbacks.text: The mandate falls on smaller employers than the current law reaches, and a small business with one or two workers out on leave at the same time can feel an absence more sharply than a large firm can.
The leave is unpaid, so many workers who cannot afford 12 weeks without a paycheck cannot use it even where they have the legal right.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial and well-defined: job protection for millions of workers facing a family or medical crisis. The cost to employers is real but modest by the bill's own evidence, and the unpaid structure keeps the government out of paying for leave while still leaving low-wage workers who cannot afford time off only partly protected.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never acted on it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Christopher Dodd introduced the bill on January 22, 1997, joined by Senators Daschle, Kennedy, Feinstein, and Kerry, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S3] [S5].
Eleven Democratic senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
The committee took no further action; the complete action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote after the referral [S5].
The bill was introduced two days after President Clinton's 1997 inauguration, when Republicans held majorities in both chambers of Congress [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 25 to 49 employees are better off, since they never had to comply with the expanded leave mandate. The 13 million workers who would have gained job-protected leave got nothing, and the bill's death removed a talking point that might have pressured Congress to act on leave policy later.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lower the Family and Medical Leave Act coverage threshold from 50 to 25 employees.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at introduction.

for.name: Sens. Edward Kennedy, Dianne Feinstein, and John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over labor law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, reported it out, or allowed a vote.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate agenda in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run committee and floor agenda never advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill died in committee without action under a Republican-led Senate.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed the 12-week unpaid leave mandate on employers currently exempt from it. These firms' interest in avoiding compliance costs ran directly against workers' interest in job-protected leave, though the bill's own findings say compliance costs for covered employers were low.

industries.industry: Larger employers already covered by the FMLA
industries.note: Employers already subject to the law gain a level playing field if smaller competitors are brought under the same rules. Their compliance obligations were unchanged by the bill.
